implementation_notes: C gives you the one-time guard and nothing else: the holder (a static pointer or struct), the acquisition call, the error state and the teardown are all hand-written. POSIX pthread_once(&once, init) with a PTHREAD_ONCE_INIT once_control, and C11 call_once(&flag, fn) with ONCE_FLAG_INIT, both guarantee that the init routine has completed before any caller returns - which is the property that makes the guard usable without a separate mutex. A plain `if (!handle) handle = acquire();` is correct only while exactly one thread (or none) can reach it; in a threaded program it is a data race that can acquire twice and leak one handle. Pick the primitive your toolchain actually provides - POSIX pthread_once or C11 call_once (see the variants); where neither exists, the remaining option is a hand-rolled acquire/release atomic guard. Release is your problem too: C has no destructor, so pair the holder with a documented teardown function (or atexit) or leak deliberately.
pitfalls: A bare `if (!res) res = acquire();` is the pattern without its guard: under threads it is an unsynchronized read/write race that can acquire the resource twice and leak all but one handle.

The init routine must not recursively call the same once_control: POSIX specifies that the inner pthread_once blocks forever, because the outer init routine cannot return while the inner call waits for it.

Neither pthread_once nor call_once can report failure - the init routine returns void - so a failed acquisition has to be recorded in the holder, and a NULL handle is otherwise indistinguishable from not-yet-initialized.
A guard reached from a library constructor (__attribute__((constructor))) races with threads the process may already own; drive lazy acquisition from code paths you control.

variants.name: C11 call_once holder
variants.implementation_notes: C11 threads.h standardizes the same guarantee: call_once(fn) calls fn exactly once even when invoked from several threads, and completion of fn synchronizes with every other call using the same flag. Prefer it when threads.h is available (glibc, musl, recent MSVC) so the code does not depend on POSIX; on targets without it, the remaining option is a hand-rolled C11 atomic guard with acquire/release ordering - which is exactly the code the standard once primitive exists to replace.
pitfalls: call_once cannot report an error: the init function returns void, so a failed acquisition must be recorded in the holder and checked by the caller.
A hand-rolled replacement must use atomic operations with acquire/release ordering; a plain pointer check compiled without atomics is a data race even on x86.
threads.h is optional in C11 and missing on some embedded toolchains - check for it rather than assuming it, or fall back to the POSIX variant.
